prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without converting it into a summary judgment motion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Court May Consider Documents Incorporated by Reference in the Complaint Without Converting Defendant's Motion Into One for Summary Judgment.**

A Rule 12(b)(6) motion ordinarily must be decided on the pleadings. If a court considers "matters outside the pleadings," Rule 12(d) requires it to treat the motion as one for summary judgment. The Ninth Circuit has long recognized that a document incorporated by reference into the complaint is not "outside" the pleadings. The court may consider it without converting the motion. *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003); *Lee v. City of Los Angeles*, 250 F.3d 668, 688–89 (9th Cir. 2001).

*A. The incorporation-by-reference doctrine is well settled in this Circuit.*

In *Branch v. Tunnell*, the court held that a district court may consider documents "whose contents are alleged in a complaint and whose authenticity no party questions, but which are not physically attached to the [plaintiff's] pleading." 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994), *overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County of Santa Clara*, 307 F.3d 1119 (9th Cir. 2002). The court later extended the doctrine to documents "whose contents are alleged in a complaint," so long as no party questions their authenticity. *Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006). It has also explained that a court "may treat such a document as part of the complaint, and thus may assume that its contents are true for purposes of a motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6)." *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908. Considering such a document does not convert the motion. *Id.*; *Lee*, 250 F.3d at 688–89.

The doctrine prevents plaintiffs from "surviv[ing] a Rule 12(b)(6) motion by deliberately omitting references to documents upon which their claims are based." *Parrino v. FHP, Inc.*, 146 F.3d 699, 706 (9th Cir. 1998) (cited with approval in *Coto Settlement v. Eisenberg*, 593 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010)). In *Coto Settlement*, the court confirmed that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference, along with judicially noticeable matters, without converting the motion. 593 F.3d at 1038. *See also Daniels-Hall v. Nat'l Educ. Ass'n*, 629 F.3d 992, 998 (9th Cir. 2010) (court may consider materials incorporated into the complaint, and "[t]he court need not accept as true allegations contradicting documents that are referenced in the complaint").

*B. The doctrine applies where the complaint refers to the document extensively or the document forms the basis of the claim.*

A defendant may invoke the doctrine "if the plaintiff refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 907. The doctrine applies to documents on which the complaint "necessarily relies." *Marder*, 450 F.3d at 448. This is so even if the plaintiff did not attach the document. *Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th Cir. 2005). In *Knievel*, the court extended the doctrine to web pages and surrounding context that the complaint referenced and that bore on the claim. *Id.* The doctrine also applies in securities cases, where courts routinely consider the full text of documents the complaint quotes in part. *In re NVIDIA Corp. Sec. Litig.*, 768 F.3d 1046, 1058 n.10 (9th Cir. 2014).

The Ninth Circuit has also set limits on the doctrine, which are met here. A court may not use it to resolve factual disputes against the plaintiff. It may not assume the truth of a document's contents when doing so would contradict well-pleaded allegations. *Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002–03 (9th Cir. 2018). A document is incorporated when the plaintiff refers to it extensively or when it forms the basis of the claim. *Id.* at 1002. *Khoja* does not limit that rule. It cautions only against using a document to dispute the complaint's well-pleaded facts. *Id.* at 1003.

*C. The documents Defendant submits satisfy the doctrine.*

The complaint quotes, relies on, and builds its claims around the documents attached to Defendant's motion. [Insert record cites: Compl. ¶¶ __.] Plaintiff cannot credibly dispute their authenticity. *See Marder*, 450 F.3d at 448; *Branch*, 14 F.3d at 454. Defendant offers them to show what they say, and the full text shows what the complaint's excerpts omit. *See Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1002. Defendant does not offer them to establish disputed facts. Because the documents are incorporated by reference, the Court may consider them under Rule 12(b)(6) without converting the motion under Rule 12(d). *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908; *Lee*, 250 F.3d at 688–89.

**Conclusion**

The Court should consider the incorporated documents and decide Defendant's motion under Rule 12(b)(6).
